reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: An X-linked heritable aortopathy: consider it particularly in males with early-onset aortic root dilatation, aneurysm and dissection
Caused by pathogenic variants in BGN, which encodes biglycan, a small leucine-rich proteoglycan of the extracellular matrix, on the X chromosome
Because inheritance is X-linked, affected males are typically more severely affected while carrier females can show milder or variable features
Aortic and arterial tortuosity and aneurysms can extend beyond the aortic root, so arterial imaging should not be confined to the heart
Connective-tissue and skeletal features overlap with other aortopathies: pectus deformity, scoliosis, joint hypermobility and a marfanoid or dysmorphic appearance
Aortic surveillance imaging is essential, with medical therapy and timely surgical repair to reduce dissection risk
Blood-pressure-lowering agents such as beta-blockers or angiotensin-pathway blockers are used as in related aortopathies
Family screening should account for the X-linked pattern when counselling relatives
reference.pathophysiology: Meester-Loeys syndrome is an X-linked heritable connective-tissue aortopathy caused by loss-of-function variants in BGN, encoding biglycan. Biglycan is a small leucine-rich proteoglycan of the extracellular matrix that helps organise collagen and elastic fibres and modulates transforming growth factor beta signalling in the arterial wall. Deficiency of functional biglycan weakens the structural integrity of the aortic media and dysregulates growth-factor signalling, predisposing to aortic root and more widespread arterial dilatation, tortuosity, aneurysm and dissection. The same matrix disturbance produces the skeletal and connective-tissue features. Because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are generally affected more severely than heterozygous females.
additionalDifferentials: Other familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography for aortic root and cardiac assessment
Whole-body magnetic resonance or CT angiography for aneurysms and tortuosity
Skeletal survey for scoliosis and chest-wall deformity
Cascade family screening informed by X-linked inheritance
redFlags: Acute chest, back or abdominal pain suggesting aortic dissection or rupture
Rapidly enlarging aortic root or other aneurysm
Signs of aortic regurgitation or cardiac decompensation
New arterial aneurysms on surveillance imaging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is dominated by the risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection, which can be life-threatening, particularly in males; structured surveillance, medical therapy and timely surgery substantially improve outcome.
pitfalls: Restricting imaging to the aortic root and missing more distal arterial disease
Failing to recognise the X-linked inheritance when counselling and screening families
Delaying surgical referral for an enlarging aneurysm
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
Consensus statements on heritable thoracic aortic disease
management: Beta-blockade and/or an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan to reduce aortic wall stress and slow aneurysm growth
Regular aortic and whole-body arterial surveillance with echocardiography and MR or CT angiography, as aneurysms extend beyond the root
Prophylactic surgical repair of the aortic root or aneurysms once size or growth thresholds are reached, ahead of dissection
Activity modification avoiding isometric straining and contact or competitive sports
Emergency recognition and management of acute aortic dissection
Manage skeletal and connective-tissue features such as scoliosis, pectus deformity and joint hypermobility with orthopaedic and physiotherapy input
Genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance with cascade family screening, noting more severe disease in males
Coordinate care through a cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery and clinical genetics multidisciplinary team
